caps: After heavy rain, a cocoa grower has about thirty minutes to scout.
Which blocks should they check first?
Guess wrong, and black pod spreads to healthy pods.
Black pod spreads by rain splash and costs an estimated twenty to thirty percent of global cocoa production.
Heavy rain is linked to lower yields in Ghana, Ecuador and Indonesia.
In Malaysia, eighty-six percent of cocoa land is smallholdings, and advisers can't visit every farm after every storm.
Growers already have photo apps, forecasts and paper logs.
But none of them turns "it rained heavily" into "walk these blocks first, in the time you have".
That's the gap KokoShield fills.
First, a borrowed university drone maps the farm's blocks.
After heavy rain, it flies again to show where water is standing, next to the rain gauge and our optional Field Node sensor.
KokoShield Field Desk combines those wet blocks, the rain reading and past cases into a ranked route that fits thirty minutes, on a phone or a printed checklist.
Scouts log each suspected pod with a note and a photo.
An adviser then confirms or rules out every case, so only verified disease counts.
In our pilot, two scouts walk the same thirty minutes on one farm: one on the ranked route, one on the usual round.
A follow-up check counts what each missed.
We go ahead only if the ranked route finds more confirmed pods per hour in three of four rounds.
Finding disease sooner means fewer pods lost, and treatment only where it's needed.
Growers use KokoShield for free; a cooperative or buyer pays seventy-five ringgit per farm per season, starting with twenty farms in Sabah or Sarawak in 2027.
We're a team of five from Universiti Malaya.
KokoShield helps cocoa growers find disease sooner after the rain: one farm first, then every cocoa region facing wetter seasons.
